caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:001169
attempts.paper_title: Distinct value computations support rapid sequential decisions
attempts.entry_title: Distinct value computations in rats' wait times and trial initiation times (Mah et al. 2023)
attempts.summary: The behavioural findings hold up: rats wait less and initiate trials faster in high-reward blocks, and wait times follow the inferred block while initiation times follow recent rewards. The model findings hold only in part, as the paper's fitting code is not public: in the agent's refits the inferential model's wait times depend on the previous offer, and rats split by inference quality lack the claimed dissociation. Comparing inferential and retrospective models was too large to run. That wait times become block-sensitive only with training could not be tested, as the dataset holds only sessions passing the inclusion criterion. With a cue before initiation, the previous block still shapes initiation times, but the previous-reward effect fails the population test.
attempts.description: Tests the behavioral findings of Mah, Schiereck, Bossio and Constantinople (2023) on dandiset 001169, which holds 23,034 sessions of 291 rats in a temporal wagering task with hidden reward blocks. It measures the block effects on wait times and trial initiation times, their dynamics at block transitions, their dependence on previous rewards, the effect of the catch probability, sex differences, and simulations of the block inference, inferential and retrospective models. The model comparison fits of Figure 3 were not run (too long), the learning analyses of Figure 4 need sessions that are not in the dandiset, and the pre-cue sessions of Figure 5 are not marked.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Mah et al. (2023) from dandiset 001169

outcomes.statement: The dataset comes from 291 rats, with a median of 33,493 behavioral trials and 71 sessions per rat.
outcomes.source: Results, Rats' deliberative and motivational decisions are sensitive to the value of the environment, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: We used a high-throughput facility to train 291 rats using computerized, semi-automated procedures. The facility generated statistically powerful datasets (median = 33,493 behavioral trials, 71 sessions).
outcomes.notes: 291 rats, median 33,493 trials and 71 sessions per rat, exactly the paper's numbers. One session of L011 is deposited twice; the medians are the same whether it is counted once or twice. The 291 include the 16 rats of the pre-initiation cue task, with their pre-cue sessions.

outcomes.statement: In mixed blocks, rats wait longer for larger offered rewards; mean wait time on catch trials rises with offer across 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 uL.
outcomes.source: Figure 1d,e; Results, Computational modeling reveals distinct value computations, paragraph 1 (Fig. 3b)
outcomes.quote: This model captured key features of the rats' behavior, including the monotonic relationship between wait time and reward offer in mixed blocks (Fig. 3b )
outcomes.notes: Population mean wait time in mixed blocks 10.45, 10.77, 11.11, 13.03 and 13.81 s from 5 to 80 uL, rising at every step. All 291 rats wait longer for 40 than 20 uL; 171 rise at every step.

outcomes.statement: Rats wait about 10% less for 20 uL in high blocks than in low blocks, across the population.
outcomes.source: Figure 1d-f; Results, Rats' deliberative and motivational decisions are sensitive to the value of the environment, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: rats adjusted how long they were willing to wait for rewards in each block, and on average waited ~10 percent less time for 20 μL in high blocks, when the opportunity cost was high, compared to in low blocks ( p ≪ 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, N = 291; Fig. 1d–f ).
outcomes.notes: Mean ratio of 20 uL wait times, high over low, 0.894 (below 1 in 279 of 291 rats). Signed-rank p = 4.61e-47 on z-scored means (Methods) and 8.18e-47 in seconds (Figure1.m), against the paper's 8.26e-49. 244 rats wait less in high blocks by the per-rat one-tailed rank-sum at p < 0.05; the paper gives no count.
deviations: The paper's MATLAB functions (wtcurves.m and the others named in each section) were rewritten in Python; the trials of each rat are concatenated over its sessions in date order, as the lab's A struct is.

outcomes.statement: Rats initiate trials more quickly in high blocks than in low blocks, across the population.
outcomes.source: Figure 1g-i; Supplementary Fig. 1; Results, Rats' deliberative and motivational decisions are sensitive to the value of the environment, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: trial initiation times were modulated by blocks in a similar pattern as the wait times, with rats initiating trials more quickly in high compared to low blocks ( p ≪ 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, N = 291; Fig. 1g–i ; Supplementary Fig. 1 ).
outcomes.notes: Mean initiation time ratio, high over low, 0.562 (below 1 in 290 of 291 rats). Signed-rank p = 1.82e-49 on z-scored means and 1.84e-49 in seconds; the paper prints 1.82e-49.

outcomes.statement: The block sensitivity of trial initiation times comes from trials after unrewarded trials; after rewarded trials initiation times do not differ between high and low blocks in the same direction.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Fig. 2b; Results, Rats' deliberative and motivational decisions are sensitive to the value of the environment, paragraph 5; Methods, Statistical analyses, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: sensitivity to the reward blocks was largely driven by initiation times following unrewarded trials (Supplementary Fig. 2 , Methods), which accounted for more variance in initiation times.

statistics.about: post-rewarded trials, high against low block
statistics.test: Wilcoxon signed-rank test (two-tailed in the legend)

statistics.about: post-unrewarded trials, high against low block
statistics.test: Wilcoxon signed-rank test (two-tailed in the legend)

statistics.about: all trials, high against low block
statistics.test: Wilcoxon signed-rank test (two-tailed in the legend)

outcomes.notes: After unrewarded trials high blocks are faster in all 291 rats (mean z difference -0.351; two-tailed p = 1.8e-49, one-tailed 9.02e-50 against the legend's 9.07e-50). After rewarded trials the one-tailed test gives p = 1 as in the legend; the two-tailed test is significant (p = 3.85e-09) in the other direction, high blocks slightly slower (+0.016 z). All trials one-tailed p = 9.12e-50 against the legend's 9.17e-50, which supports reading the legend's p values as the code's one-tailed tests.

outcomes.statement: Wait times show no major differences after rewarded and after unrewarded trials.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Fig. 3; Results, Rats' deliberative and motivational decisions are sensitive to the value of the environment, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: There were no major differences in wait times following rewarded or unrewarded trials (Supplementary Fig. 3 ).
outcomes.notes: Mean 20 uL wait time ratio 0.899 after rewarded and 0.897 after unrewarded trials; difference 0.0022, signed-rank p = 0.636.

outcomes.statement: After a transition into a mixed block, wait times converge to a common value whether the previous block was high or low, while trial initiation times in mixed blocks keep depending on the previous block (slower after high blocks, faster after low blocks).
outcomes.source: Figure 2a,b; Supplementary Figs 4 and 5; Results, Trial initiation and wait times exhibited distinct temporal dynamics, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: In mixed blocks, the wait times following high and low blocks converged to a common value, regardless of the previous block type ... Trial initiation times, however, showed longer timescale effects such that initiation times in mixed blocks strongly depended on the previous block identity (Fig. 2b ; Supplementary Fig. 4 ).
outcomes.notes: The wait time gap between curves after high and after low blocks over trials 1 to 20 is 0.325 of its size over trials -20 to -1 (0.082 over 10 to 20); for initiation times it is 2.31 times that size with the code's pooled detrending and 1.97 with the Methods' per-session detrending (2.42 and 2.06 over 10 to 20). Mixed-block initiation time is higher after high blocks (z +0.053 against -0.072) in all 291 rats, signed-rank p = 1.8e-49; the same with transitions counted within sessions only.
deviations: The mixed-block means of part (2) follow FigureS4.m, which finds transitions on the concatenated trials, so a session that starts in a mixed block after one that ended in a high or low block counts as a transition; a variant counting transitions within sessions gives the same result.
The smoothing follows MATLAB's smooth (an even span reduced by one, shrinking at the ends), ignoring NaNs, a standard choice.

outcomes.statement: Longer timescale contrast effects also appear at transitions from mixed into high or low blocks for trial initiation times, but not for wait times.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Fig. 5; Results, Trial initiation and wait times exhibited distinct temporal dynamics, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: These longer timescale dynamics, which are reminiscent of incentive contrast effects 29 , were also evident in the transitions from mixed blocks into high/low blocks for trial initiation times, but not wait times (Supplementary Fig. 5 )
outcomes.notes: Over trials -20 to -1 the initiation curve before a low block is above the one before a high block (+0.062 pooled detrending, +0.049 per session; 276 and 261 of 291 rats). Relative to their gap after the transition, wait time curves differ less (0.134) than initiation curves (0.244 and 0.204).

outcomes.statement: In mixed blocks, wait times are explained by the current offer and barely by previous offers, while trial initiation times reflect an exponentially decaying effect of previous rewards (larger recent rewards, faster initiation).
outcomes.source: Figure 2c,d; Results, Trial initiation and wait times exhibited distinct temporal dynamics, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Examination of the regression coefficients revealed qualitatively different dynamics, in which the wait times were explained by the reward offered on the current trial, but the trial initiation times reflected an exponentially weighted effect of previous rewards
outcomes.notes: Mean current offer coefficient for wait time +0.211 (95% interval of the mean +0.204 to +0.218), larger in size than every previous coefficient (within 0.004 of 0 after zeroing, within 0.013 before). Initiation coefficients 1, 2 and 3 trials back -0.030, -0.023 and -0.010, negative and shrinking, with 10 or 9 previous rewards and before or after zeroing. 250 of 291 rats have a negative lag-1 coefficient.
deviations: The 95% interval across rats is taken as the t interval of the mean over rats; the claims file does not say which interval.

Regressions use log2 of the male volumes, as the claims file's common method says; the code (log2(A.reward)) uses the raw volumes, so female volumes would enter as 4 to 64 uL. The first run used the raw volumes; the numbers moved by at most 0.001.

outcomes.statement: The time constants of exponential fits to the previous trial coefficients differ between trial initiation times and wait times, with longer time constants for initiation times (wait time time constants are mostly 0).
outcomes.source: Figure 2e; Results, Trial initiation and wait times exhibited distinct temporal dynamics, paragraph 2; Methods, Trial history effects
outcomes.quote: We fit exponential curves to the previous trial coefficients for each rat, and found that the distributions of exponential decay time constant parameters ( τ ) were significantly different for the trial initiation and wait times ( p ≪ 0.01, Wilcoxon sign-rank test, N = 291; Fig. 2e ).
outcomes.notes: Signed-rank p = 1.25e-45 (Methods' reading) and 2.28e-44 (code's reading), against the paper's 1.3e-49. Mean initiation tau 2.06 and 2.03, mean wait time tau 0.066 and 0.098; the wait time tau is 0 in 248 of 291 rats, the initiation tau in 18 and 26. 267 and 261 rats have a larger initiation tau. Offers are the male volumes (see fig2c-d).
deviations: The exponential is fitted by an exact least-squares profile (D solved for each tau on a grid within the bounds, then a bounded search over tau) in place of fmincon from 10 random starts. A gradient search from random starts was tried while preparing and stalled at D = 0 in many rats, where the error does not depend on tau; the profile finds the optimum the random starts look for.

outcomes.statement: Across rats, the time constants for wait times and trial initiation times are not correlated.
outcomes.source: Figure 2f; Results, Trial initiation and wait times exhibited distinct temporal dynamics, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Moreover, τ parameters were not correlated across models ( r = 0.08, p = 0.18, Pearson linear correlation, N = 291, Fig. 2f ).

statistics.about: as printed in the Figure 2f legend

outcomes.notes: Pearson r = -0.033, p = 0.572 (Methods' taus) and r = +0.023, p = 0.693 (code's taus), both far from significance; the first is close to the legend's r = -0.03, p = 0.53, while the second has the opposite sign, near 0. The Results print r = 0.08, p = 0.18.

outcomes.statement: Rats split by fast or slow temporal integration of initiation times (tau below the 20th or above the 80th percentile) differ in their initiation time regression coefficients but not in their wait time coefficients.
outcomes.source: Figure 2g,h; Results, Trial initiation and wait times exhibited distinct temporal dynamics, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: There were differences in temporal integration for trial initiation times, but not wait times, for these groups (Fig. 2g, h trial initiation time p < 0.05, wait time p = 0.1, permutation test, N = 116).

statistics.about: initiation time coefficients, fast against slow group
wait time coefficients, fast against slow group

outcomes.notes: 58 rats per group (N = 116 as in the paper). Initiation coefficients p = 0.000 with either reading of the taus (paper 0.02; observed taus 0.91 and 3.90 for fast and slow); wait time coefficients p = 0.187 and 0.200 (paper 0.1), not significant. myTauShuffleTest.m fits every coefficient but the constant, so the wait time test includes the current offer coefficient (0.19 to 0.23), and every shuffled wait time fit has D at its bound of 1. Variants, not the paper's test - with the 9 previous coefficients only, p = 0.223 and 0.235 (0.249 and 0.260 with the observed fits on the shuffle scale), 14 to 15% of shuffled fits at the bound; with the current coefficient and the observed fits on the shuffle scale, p = 0.000, with every fit at the bound. The absence is judged on the paper's test.
deviations: Exponential fits as in fig2e-tau-differ (exact profile in place of random starts), inside the shuffle test.
Offers are the male volumes (see fig2c-d).

outcomes.statement: In mixed blocks, wait times for 20 uL do not depend on whether the previous offer was smaller or larger than 20 uL, for 87% of rats (253 of 291) and for the population.
outcomes.source: Figure 2j; Results, Trial initiation and wait times exhibited distinct temporal dynamics, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Indeed, for almost all rats (87%), wait times for 20 μL offers in mixed blocks were not significantly different if they were preceded by rewards that were smaller or larger than 20 μL ( p > 0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, N = 253/291).
outcomes.notes: 38 of 291 rats have p < 0.05, so 253 do not, the paper's count. Population z -0.007 after smaller and +0.005 after larger offers; rank-sum on per-rat means p = 0.708, signed-rank variant p = 0.808 (paper 0.8).
deviations: The previous trial is the one before in the concatenated data, which may be in another block or session, as waittime_20ul_by_previous_vol.m takes it (rew(find_20ul_catch-1)).

outcomes.statement: In mixed blocks, trial initiation times are slower after offers smaller than 20 uL than after offers larger than 20 uL, significantly so for 89% of rats (256 of 291) and for the population.
outcomes.source: Figure 2k; Results, Trial initiation and wait times exhibited distinct temporal dynamics, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: However, for 89% of rats, trial initiation times were significantly modulated by previous rewards, suggesting fixed and incrementally updated estimates of the value of the environment, respectively ( p < 0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, N = 256/291, Fig. 2i–l ).
outcomes.notes: All mixed-block trials (the code) give 255 rats with p < 0.05, all slower after smaller offers; population z +0.099 against -0.149, rank-sum p = 9.34e-97, signed-rank p = 1.84e-49 (legend 1.84e-49). 20 uL trials only (the Methods) give 265 rats with p < 0.05, 202 of them slower after smaller offers and 63 faster, population +0.000 against -0.083, rank-sum p = 9.71e-25. The paper's count ("significantly modulated") does not name a direction, so both readings match; counted in the claimed direction, the Methods' 202 would be below 256 - 26.

outcomes.statement: Sensitivity to the previous offer is larger for trial initiation times than for wait times across rats.
outcomes.source: Figure 2l; Methods, Trial history effects
outcomes.quote: We compared wait time and trial initiation time sensitivity to previous offers across rats using a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
outcomes.notes: Mean sensitivity +0.248 for initiation (code's reading) against -0.012 for wait times, signed-rank p = 6.09e-38 (paper 6.21e-38); +0.083 and p = 2.19e-08 under the Methods' reading.

outcomes.statement: Satiety effects on trial initiation times are modest, and the results, including the dynamics at block transitions, do not change qualitatively without detrending.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Fig. 6; Results, Trial initiation and wait times exhibited distinct temporal dynamics, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: However, there was no qualitative change in any of our results, including the dynamics at block transitions, if we did not detrend (Supplementary Fig. 6 ).
outcomes.notes: Without detrending, initiation over trials 1 to 20 of mixed blocks is +0.147 after high and -0.109 after low blocks, higher after high in all 291 rats; part (2) of fig2a does not detrend and holds (p = 1.8e-49). The trend removed by detrending has a median of 0.05 z per 100 trials.

outcomes.statement: Rats' wait times in mixed blocks depend in a graded way on the catch probability, as the wait time model predicts (shorter waits at higher catch probability).
outcomes.source: Figure 3c; Results, Computational modeling reveals distinct value computations, paragraph 1; Methods, Statistical analyses, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: as well as a graded dependence of wait times on the catch probability (Fig. 3c )
outcomes.notes: Rats with data at 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25 and 0.35 number 3, 188, 61, 151 and 40, all within tolerance. Mean wait time decreases from 0.15 to 0.2 to 0.25 at all 5 offers (20 uL 12.10, 11.08, 10.61 s). The dandiset also has catch probability 0.3 in 360 sessions of 8 rats, a value the paper does not list. By each rat's most common probability the counts are 107, 42, 126, 6 (0.3) and 10, so the paper's counts are rats with data at each probability. wtByPCatch.m does not ask for an opt-out; 140 catch trials over all rats have a wait time without one, and with opt-out trials only the 20 uL means are the same to 0.01 s and the decrease holds at all 5 offers.
deviations: The catch probability of each trial is taken from the raw trial table (catch_percentage), as the processed table has none; the two tables are the same trials row by row.

outcomes.statement: A retrospective model with a learning rate scaled by changes in the inferred block posterior captures the slow and fast dynamics of trial initiation times at block transitions and their dependence on previous rewards, while a static learning rate or an unsigned prediction error gain does not.
outcomes.source: Figure 3g-i; Supplementary Fig. 7; Results, Computational modeling reveals distinct value computations, paragraphs 3 and 4
outcomes.quote: We explored versions of the dynamic learning rate that did not reflect inference, including using the unsigned reward prediction error or a running average of reward prediction errors 38 . However, these models could not capture both short and long timescale dynamics at block transitions (Supplementary Fig. 7 ).
outcomes.notes: On rat J004's trials (as Figure3.m and FigureS7.m simulate), the Equation 10 model shows an overshoot (+0.016 with noise variance 8, +0.081 with 4) and a persistent post-high above post-low gap (+0.239, +0.287). The static learning rate lacks one feature at alpha_0 0.05 and 0.4 but shows both at 0.8 (gap +0.0041 with noise, -0.0001 without). The unsigned prediction error gain lacks the gap at 0.05 but shows both at 0.4 and 0.8, with gaps +0.012 and +0.006 (+0.025 and +0.013 without noise). The criterion, which sets no threshold, asks each alternative to lack one feature at every alpha_0, which fails at three of six settings, so the alternatives' part holds only in part. Controls added in revision - a noise-only flat time gives mean overshoots of +0.011 to +0.019 (95th percentiles +0.029 to +0.058) and gap 95th percentiles of +0.010 to +0.020. Judged against these, every alternative lacks one feature at every alpha_0, and the Equation 10 model shows both at noise 4 but not at noise 8 (overshoot +0.016 against +0.046). Without noise or smoothing, all models overshoot (+0.43 for Equation 10, +0.21 to +0.31 for the alternatives at 0.4 and 0.8) and the alternatives at 0.4 and 0.8 show gaps of +0.11 to +0.21 against +1.24. The two controls point different ways, and the outcome follows the criterion as written. For Fig. 3i, the model's initiation times are higher after offers below 20 uL (+0.052 z) than above (-0.049 z) in 290 of 291 rats, as the rats' are.
deviations: For the Fig. 3i part, Figure3.m simulates each rat with its own retrospective parameters fitted to wait times, which are not in the dandiset (they are in the Zenodo deposit) and were not refitted (see fig3j). J004's parameters (alpha_0 0.1042, D 0.2527) are used for every rat, an assumption. The direction does not depend on alpha_0 - without noise, the model is higher after offers below 20 uL at every alpha_0 from 0.01 to 0.8 tried (by +0.077 to +1.076 z on average; in 273 of 291 rats at 0.01 and 290 or 291 at the others).

Each script's own scaling of D, initial kappa and reset at session starts is used (D times 25, 10 and 15; kappa starting at mean(log(rewards)), 20 and 0.5), as GenerateLatencyData_AlphaPHModel.m, _VanillaAlpha.m and _RPEAlpha.m set them. The static model averages 10 noise draws per trial, as its script does.
The overshoot and gap measures are the claims file's; their signs only are judged, so values near 0 decide the alternatives' part.

outcomes.statement: In simulations of a Bayes optimal observer, hearing the reward offer reduces the uncertainty of beliefs about the hidden block (posterior variance below prior variance).
outcomes.source: Results, Reducing state uncertainty did not change trial initiation times, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Model simulations of a Bayes' optimal observer did show that the reward offer reduced the uncertainty of subjective beliefs about the hidden state (comparing variance of prior to variance of posterior, p ≪ 0.001, Wilcoxon sign-rank test).
outcomes.notes: With the code's and Equation 6's transition matrices, the posterior is less uncertain than the prior in every rat under both readings. Variance of block probabilities rises from 0.157 to 0.169 and variance of block value falls from 0.104 to 0.082 (code's matrix), per-rat signed-rank p = 1.8e-49 for each; over the trials of J004 p = 5.31e-257 and p = 0, and over all rats' 6,037,811 trials pooled p = 0 for both readings (mean change +0.0124 and -0.0222).
deviations: The inference follows GenerateSynthData_Bayes.m (trials with a wait time; belief reset to 1/2, 1/4, 1/4 at session starts, where there is no prior). The code's transition matrix moves from mixed to high or low with H0/2 each, where Equation 6 gives H0; both were run.
Under the reading by variance of the block probabilities, a less uncertain posterior has a larger variance, so the test is for an increase there and a decrease for the variance of block value.

outcomes.statement: Male and female rats do not differ in their wait time ratios or trial initiation time ratios.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Fig. 12; Methods, Training for male and female rats
outcomes.quote: We did not observe any significant differences between the male and female rats, in terms of contextual effects, or behavioral dynamics at block transitions (Supplementary Fig. 12 ).
outcomes.notes: 184 males and 107 females from the subject metadata. Wait time ratios 0.892 against 0.898 (rank-sum p = 0.238, paper 0.23); initiation ratios 0.563 against 0.559 (p = 0.557, paper 0.59).

outcomes.statement: Without removing wait times more than 1 SD above the pooled mean, the contextual effects on wait times are qualitatively similar, with longer average wait times, mainly in low blocks.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Fig. 14; Methods, Statistical analyses, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Wait time curves without threshold (right) have qualitatively similar context effects, but longer average wait times.
outcomes.notes: Unthresholded 20 uL wait time 12.51 s in high against 14.47 s in low blocks, signed-rank p = 1.02e-43. The unthresholded mean is longer at all 11 offer and block combinations, by 2.31 to 2.86 s in low blocks and 0.95 to 1.78 s in mixed blocks. The low block curve is flatter unthresholded (0.12 against 0.67 s from 5 to 20 uL).

outcomes.statement: The rats and switch dates that the paper's Figure5.m lists mark which of the dandiset's sessions were run on the pre-initiation cue task, which nothing in the files marks.
outcomes.source: Methods, Pre-initiation cue task; Figure5.m (github.com/constantinoplelab/published at b7b68ca8c107, rat_behavior/Figures/Figure5.m, ratListAll and startDates)
outcomes.quote: To modulate the subjective uncertainty in the rat’s estimate of state (block) before trial initiation time, we ran a subset of rats on a variation of the task where we cued reward offer before rats initiated a trial ( N = 16).
outcomes.notes: 14 of 16 rats are linked. After the switch date their initiation times depend on the current offer (ANOVA p < 0.05, slopes -0.041 to -0.090 z per doubling of the offer); before it no switched rat reaches p < 0.05 (slopes -0.011 to +0.014). S042 (p = 0.151) and S050 (p = 0.597) are not confirmed; they have 25 and 11 sessions after the date in the dandiset. All sessions are protocol RWTautowait2, so nothing in the files marks the task change.
deviations: Figure5.m lists 16 rats and 20 start dates; its loop indexes startDates(rr), so the first 16 dates are paired with the rats in order, as here.
The rule for a linked rat was written after a first look at the same check while preparing.

outcomes.statement: With the reward cue played before trial initiation, trial initiation times become sensitive to the offered reward.
outcomes.source: Figure 5b; Results, Reducing state uncertainty did not change trial initiation times, paragraph 3; Methods, Pre-initiation cue task
outcomes.quote: Their trial initiation times became sensitive to the offered reward (Fig. 5b ).
outcomes.notes: Population mean z-scored initiation time on pre-cue sessions falls at every step from 5 to 80 uL (+0.102 to -0.126 from the switch date; +0.117 to -0.152 after 30 pre-cue sessions), and is flat on the original task (0.000 to -0.012). ANOVA p < 0.05 in 14 of 16 rats on the pre-cue task (11 of 11 rats with sessions after 30 pre-cue sessions) and 0 of 12 on the original task. The link holds for 14 rats; the two not confirmed are the two without a significant ANOVA here, so the count of 14 rests on the linked rats. The same ANOVA validates the link (pre-cue-session-link) and is reported here, so the two are not independent; the switch dates come from Figure5.m, not from the data.
deviations: The Methods use every session of these rats, without the inclusion criterion; the dandiset holds only the sessions that pass it, so some pre-cue sessions are missing.
The Methods' reading (after 30 pre-cue sessions) counts the dandiset's sessions, which leaves 7 of the 12 switched rats with any.

outcomes.statement: On the pre-initiation cue task, trial initiation times for 20 uL in mixed blocks are still modulated by the previous reward, for 13 of 16 rats and for the population.
outcomes.source: Figure 5c; Results, Reducing state uncertainty did not change trial initiation times, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: However, trial initiation times for 20μL in mixed blocks were still modulated by the previous reward, consistent with the use of incrementally updated estimates of the value of the environment within a block ( p < 0.05 for 13/16 rats; Fig. 5c ).
outcomes.notes: Under the reading the Fig. 5c legend gives ("behavior on trials offering 20μL conditioned on the previous reward offer"), sessions from the switch date, 14 of 16 rats have p < 0.05 (expected 13 +- 1), 9 of them slower after smaller offers; 11 of 16 rats are slower after smaller offers, and the population rank-sum gives p = 0.0676 (signed-rank 0.0182), not below 0.001. The count matches, the population test does not. With all mixed-block trials (Figure5.m), 13 rats have p < 0.05, all 16 are slower after smaller offers, p = 1.86e-06 (paper 1.03e-4); with the trials after violations left out, which repeat the previous offer while the cued current offer drives initiation on this task (fig5b), the mean is lower after smaller offers (-0.108 against -0.072 z), 5 rats are slower after smaller offers and p = 0.30. After 30 pre-cue sessions 11 rats remain (9 with p < 0.05 and p = 0.000182 with all trials; 10 and p = 0.47 with 20 uL trials). Changed from reproduced after the round 1 verification. Added after round 2 - within a session and block every post-violation trial repeats the previous offer (share 1.000 in all 16 rats; 0.985 to 0.996 over all post-violation trials, against 0.195 to 0.226 after other trials). The only post-violation trials that do not repeat are a session's first trials, whose previous trial in the concatenated data ends the previous session; dropping post-violation trials from the 20 uL test removes 455 of its 18,075 trials, all of them session first trials, with mean z initiation time +2.920 against -0.057, and moves p from 0.0676 to 0.611. The 14 significant rats include 5 in the opposite direction and three with mean differences near 0 (E008 +0.0007, S042 -0.0073, M044 -0.0173), so the count is weak support.
deviations: The 20 uL reading of the Fig. 5c legend is adopted (an assumption between the readings the criterion lists). The all-trials reading of Figure5.m matches the claim only through the post-violation trials, which carry the previous offer into the current one on a task where the current offer drives initiation time.
Only sessions that pass the inclusion criterion are in the dandiset (see fig5b).

outcomes.statement: On the pre-initiation cue task, how quickly rats initiate trials in mixed blocks still depends on the previous block.
outcomes.source: Figure 5d; Results, Reducing state uncertainty did not change trial initiation times, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Moreover, how quickly they initiated trials in mixed blocks continued to depend on the previous block identity (Fig. 5d ).
outcomes.notes: Over trials 1 to 20 of mixed blocks on pre-cue sessions, z-scored initiation time is +0.149 after high and -0.132 after low blocks, higher after high in all 16 rats, signed-rank p = 3.05e-05; the same with per-session detrending and after 30 pre-cue sessions (11 of 11 rats, p = 0.000977).
deviations: Only sessions that pass the inclusion criterion are in the dandiset (see fig5b).

outcomes.statement: Wait times are better fit by the inferential model, which uses hidden state inference to choose a block-specific value of the environment, than by the retrospective model, by BIC, AIC and cross-validated negative log-likelihood.
outcomes.source: Figure 3j; Supplementary Fig. 8a,c,e; Results, Computational modeling reveals distinct value computations, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: By several model comparison metrics, wait times were better fit by the inferential model that used hidden state inference to select block-specific estimates of the value of the environment ( p ≪ 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, N = 291; Fig. 3j , Supplementary Fig. 8 )
outcomes.notes: The refit needs each rat's wait times fitted by the inferential and retrospective models with 100 random starts (Methods, Fitting and evaluating models), on all data and on 5 folds. Revised after the round 1 verification - with the retrospective likelihood compiled (numba), one evaluation on J004 takes 0.157 ms (19.9 ms in pure Python), and an inferential fit with 100 starts takes 0.68 s per rat (fig3f). From the 192 evaluations per start counted in those fits, the refit on all data and 5 folds is estimated at 2.68 h on one core for the retrospective model (0.67 h on 4) and 0.66 h for the inferential and belief state models, about 3.3 h in all, beyond the notebook limit of 1 h with the 24.0 minutes the notebook already takes. These are the numbers of the final run; the timings depend on the machine, and the verifier's round 2 re-execution gave 0.253 ms, 1.24 s per rat, 4.32 h (1.08 h on 4) and 1.20 h, about 5.5 h in all, with a notebook of 45.3 minutes. The first run's estimate, 138 h in the author's run and 162 h in the verifier's round 1 re-execution, timed a pure Python loop and an assumed 200 evaluations per start. The fitting code is not in the paper's repository, so the trials in the likelihood, the bounds, the starting ranges and the folds are also open. The paper's fits are in the Zenodo deposit (doi:10.5281/zenodo.10031483) as BestFit.mat files of about 1.1 GB each inside a 12.4 GB zip; using them would test the paper's fits, not the dandiset, and was not tried.

outcomes.statement: Model comparison does not distinguish the inferential model from the belief state model for wait times.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Fig. 8b,d,f; Results, Computational modeling reveals distinct value computations, paragraph 6
outcomes.quote: In fact, when the posterior beliefs are stable, which is often the case, the belief state and inferential models are identical, and model comparison did not favor one model over the other (Supplementary Fig. 8 ).
outcomes.notes: Needs the belief state model fitted as in fig3j, on all data and 5 folds, beside the inferential fits; not run with fig3j (estimated at 3.3 h on one core in all in the final run, 5.5 h in the verifier's round 2 re-execution).

outcomes.statement: Wait times predicted by the inferential model fitted to each rat are, like the rats' wait times, not sensitive to the previous offer for 20 uL in mixed blocks.
outcomes.source: Figure 3f; Results, Computational modeling reveals distinct value computations, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Across rats, the model also captured that wait times for 20μL in mixed blocks were not sensitive to previous rewards (Fig 2j ; Fig. 3f ).
outcomes.notes: The inferential model of GenerateSynthData_Bayes.m fitted to each rat (100 random starts) predicts wait times, one noisy draw as Figure3.m uses, that are longer after offers below 20 uL (+0.033 z) than above (-0.032 z); rank-sum on per-rat means p = 9.52e-11 (signed-rank 3.51e-09), so by the claim's test the model is sensitive to the previous offer. Without noise the difference is +0.448 z (p = 1.49e-68). The rats' own difference is -0.012 z. The effect comes from the mixed-block trials the model labels high or low (median 8.5% per rat), with kappa_high > kappa_mixed > kappa_low in 197 of 291 rats. It is small (+0.065 z, about a quarter of the rats' initiation time sensitivity of +0.248 z), and 16 rats reach p < 0.05 against the rats' 38. On J004 the fit recovers its generating parameters to within 0.004. 6 of 291 fits have a parameter within 1e-4 of a bound. Changed from blocked after the round 1 verification, which found the fit feasible.
deviations: The fitting code is not in the paper's repository. The model and its parameter scaling follow GenerateSynthData_Bayes.m (params in [0, 1], kappa = params C log2(min reward) / tau, D = 10 params, R = log2 of the raw volume, C = max(1 - catch probability), tau = 2.5 s) and the noise the Methods give (log-normal, variance 8). The likelihood is taken over opt-out catch trials, the trials where the wait time is the rat's choice, an assumption.
scipy's bounded L-BFGS-B from 100 random starts in place of fmincon from 100 random seeds (Methods, Fitting and evaluating models).

outcomes.statement: Within mixed blocks, wait times for 20 uL differ between trials the inferential model labels as high and as low blocks, so wait times reflect mistaken inferences.
outcomes.source: Supplementary Fig. 9; Results, Computational modeling reveals distinct value computations, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: The rats' wait times reflected these mistaken inferences, further indicating that their wait times were well-described by the inferential model ( p ≪ 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing wait times for 20μL in misinferred high vs. low blocks, N = 291; Supplementary Fig. 9 ).
outcomes.notes: On 20 uL catch trials in mixed blocks, mean wait time is 10.85 s on trials the model labels high and 11.90 s on trials it labels low, shorter when labelled high in 230 of 291 rats, signed-rank p = 9.72e-23 (Equation 6's matrix 238 rats, p = 2.57e-25). The claim depends on fig3j in the claims file because the labels come from the inferential model, but the labels come from the block inference alone, which has no fitted parameter. Changed from blocked after the round 1 verification.
deviations: FigureS9.m takes the labels on held-out test sets, whose folds are not given. The labels on all sessions are used, which are the test-set labels when the folds are whole sessions, since the inference is reset at every session (an assumption).
Wait times on catch trials as FigureS9.m takes them, without asking for an opt-out.

outcomes.statement: Rats with optimal and poor inference (high or low lambda of the sub-optimal inferential model) differ in their wait time dynamics at transitions from mixed into low or high blocks, but not in their trial initiation time dynamics.
outcomes.source: Figure 3l; Supplementary Figs 10 and 11; Results, Computational modeling reveals distinct value computations, paragraph 7
outcomes.quote: Rats with optimal and poor inference exhibited significantly different dynamics at transitions from mixed into low or high blocks, indicated by different inverse temperature parameters (mix to low/high, p < 0.05, one-tailed permutation test, N = 180 Fig. 3l ). There was no difference in the dynamics of trial initiation times for those same groups of rats (mixed to low... p = 0.3, mixed to high... p = 0.2, one-tailed permutation test, N = 180; Fig. 3l ).

statistics.about: wait time, mixed to low, slope (legend)
wait time, mixed to high, right asymptote (legend)
trial initiation time, mixed to low, slope (legend; p = 0.3 in the Results)
trial initiation time, mixed to high, right asymptote (legend; p = 0.2 in the Results)

outcomes.notes: The fitted lambdas pile up at the bounds (59 rats at 0, 69 at 1, median 0.775), so the 20th and 80th percentiles are 0 and 1 and the groups are the rats at them (59 and 69, N = 128 against 116). At mixed to low the wait time slope C does not differ (shuffle p = 0.242; 0.197 with the 40/60 split), which the criterion needs. At mixed to high the wait time upper asymptote D differs (p = 0.000 under both splits) but C does not (0.355, 0.237). Initiation times also differ in D at mixed to high (p = 0.028; 0.007 with per-session detrending, 0.006 with the 40/60 split), so their absence fails under the legend's reading; their C does not differ (0.129 to 0.494). Neither reading holds under either split. Changed from blocked after the round 1 verification. The paper's 20/80 split gives N = 116, which ties at the bounds could not give, so the refit's lambdas are not distributed as the paper's, and the groups here come from a tie-break, not the paper's rule; the failure may be the refit's and cannot be separated from it. The 40/60 split, which has no ties, also fails.
deviations: The sub-optimal model follows GenerateSynthData_Bayes_subopt_onlylambda_flat.m and is fitted with the likelihood of fig3f (opt-out catch trials, log-normal noise of variance 8), an assumption, as the fitting code is not public.

The likelihood changes with lambda only in steps, so lambda is profiled over 41 values from 0 to 1 and the other 4 parameters fitted at each (2 starts, one warm-started), in place of fmincon from 100 random starts.

Figure3.m forms the groups with strict inequalities (lambda above or below the percentile); with ties at 0 and 1 both groups would be empty, so the rats at the percentile join the group (a tie-break).

Logistic fits with scipy's bounded least_squares from 10 random starts in place of fmincon (my_fit_sigmoid.m), with its bounds; transition curves with 30 trials either side and 10-trial smoothing (Figure3.m).

outcomes.statement: When the hidden blocks are introduced, wait times for 20 uL become sensitive to the block only gradually over training, while trial initiation times are block sensitive from the first session.
outcomes.source: Figure 4a,b; Results, Block sensitivity for wait times requires structure learning, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: In the final stage of training, when rats were introduced to the hidden states, their wait times for 20μL gradually became sensitive to the reward block (Fig. 4a ) ... In contrast, trial initiation times exhibited block sensitivity on the first session in the final training stage (Fig. 4a ).
outcomes.notes: Fig. 4 uses all stage 8 sessions, including those that fail the inclusion criterion (Methods, Learning dynamics); Figure4.m reads them from the lab's S structs. The dandiset was converted from A_Structs_Final (the conversion script constantinople-lab-to-nwb, mah_2024_convert_all_sessions.py), which holds only the sessions the lab's parser keeps after screen_perf.m. The S structs are not in the Zenodo deposit, which holds A_Structs_Final, A_Structs_all and the model fits. A_Structs_all was not read here; whether it holds the excluded sessions is not known. A partial test on the included sessions was not run: the claims are about how behavior changes from the first stage 8 sessions, which are the ones the criterion removes, so a trend over the included sessions would test a different selection.

outcomes.statement: The effect of the previous reward on trial initiation times is comparable early and late in training.
outcomes.source: Figure 4c; Results, Block sensitivity for wait times requires structure learning, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: This sensitivity was comparable early and late in training, consistent with animals using previous rewards to a similar extent at these timepoints (Fig. 4c ).
outcomes.notes: As fig4a-wait-time-block-sensitivity-emerges; the sessions that fail the inclusion criterion are not in the dandiset. A partial test on the included sessions was not run: the claims are about how behavior changes from the first stage 8 sessions, which are the ones the criterion removes, so a trend over the included sessions would test a different selection.

outcomes.statement: The overshoot of trial initiation times after transitions from high to mixed blocks becomes more prominent with training, on a timescale like that of block sensitivity for wait times.
outcomes.source: Figure 4d,e; Results, Block sensitivity for wait times requires structure learning, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: The overshoot became more prominent with training (Fig. 4d ), on a similar timescale as block sensitivity for wait times (Fig. 4e ), suggesting a shared mechanism.
outcomes.notes: As fig4a-wait-time-block-sensitivity-emerges; the first stage 8 sessions, including those excluded by the criterion, are not in the dandiset. A partial test on the included sessions was not run: the claims are about how behavior changes from the first stage 8 sessions, which are the ones the criterion removes, so a trend over the included sessions would test a different selection.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds only the sessions that pass the paper's inclusion criterion (it was converted from the lab's A_Structs_Final), which neither its description nor its files say. The sessions that fail it, which the paper's learning analyses (Fig. 4) and pre-cue analyses (Fig. 5) use, are not in it.

Nothing marks the sessions run on the pre-initiation cue task. The 16 rats of Fig. 5 are among the 291, their pre-cue sessions are included, and all sessions have protocol RWTautowait2. The switch dates in the paper's Figure5.m mark them for 14 of the 16 rats, as initiation times depend on the current offer only after the date.
One session is deposited twice, sub-L011_ses-RWTautowait2-20221004-095612.nwb and the same name with a "-x" suffix, with identical trial data.

The processed trial table has no catch probability. The conversion maps the A struct field under the misspelled name prob_cacth, so prob_catch is dropped; the value is only in the raw trial table (catch_percentage), which has the same rows.

The raw trial table's is_catch differs from the processed is_catch on 176,009 trials; the processed flag is reward_delay == 100, as the lab's parser defines it, and the raw flag is set on trials with ordinary delays. Neither description says which to use.
The subject age is empty in 21,853 of 23,034 files and is the range P6M/P24M in the others, so no rat's age is given.
360 sessions of 8 rats have catch probability 0.3, which is not among the five cohorts the paper lists (0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.35).

The code that fits the wait time models (inferential, belief state, sub-optimal and retrospective) is not in the paper's repository, which loads the fits from files. Question for the authors - which trials enter the likelihood (opt-out catch trials only, as assumed here for fig3f and fig3l, or hit trials as censored), what bounds and starting ranges are used, and how the 5 folds are formed (whole sessions, as assumed here for suppfig9, or trials)?

Equation 6 lets a mixed block become a low (or high) block with probability H0, while every model script uses H0/2 for each (p_b in GenerateSynthData_Bayes.m). Question for the authors - which was used for the fits? Both give the same outcome for the Bayes observer claim here.

Figure5.m lists 16 rats but 20 start dates, and the Methods' 30-session offset for switched rats is not in it; the code uses the first 16 dates. Question for the authors - are the dates paired with the rats in order, and were sessions before the 30th pre-cue session left out?
The correlation of the two time constants is r = 0.08, p = 0.18 in the Results and r = -0.03, p = 0.53 in the Figure 2f legend; this attempt finds r = -0.032 and +0.023 under the two readings.

myTauShuffleTest.m refits the shuffled groups' mean coefficients times 10 with D at most 1, and the observed groups' coefficients unscaled; for wait times the coefficients include the current offer (about 0.2, so about 2 after scaling), and every shuffled fit sits at the bound, so the null is not on the observed scale. The Methods describe the fits on previous trial coefficients only. Question for the authors - was the wait time test meant to include the current offer?

verifications.reviewed: The first executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper's full text (PMC10663503). The verifier checked the archive's metadata for the blocked claims and tested helpers on synthetic inputs (fit_exp_decay, zero_after_first_ns, transition_codes, lognormal_noise, matlab_smooth). It could not read the paper's MATLAB code.

disagreements.reason: Code reading by date - 13 of 16 rats, p = 1.9e-6, which passes. Methods reading (20 uL trials, as the Fig. 5c legend says) - 14 of 16 rats but rank-sum p = 0.068 by date and 0.47 after 30 sessions, which fails. On the pre-cue task the code reading is confounded - post-violation trials repeat the previous offer (Methods, Pre-initiation cue task), and on this task the current cued offer drives initiation time; the notebook does not mention this confound.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (verifier-2; same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook of the author-revise-1 run, re-executed by the verifier, the helper module, the claims file and this record, with the paper. Report in transcripts/mah-2023/verifier-2-report.md. The verifier agrees with all 33 outcomes. It found stale timings for fig3j and suppfig8 in the record and the Summary, a stale loading time in cell 2 and the README, a wrong statement on the fig2f readings, an unbacked deviation in fig3i, an unverified premise in fig5c and a missing caveat in fig3l. After it, two cells were added (fig3i over alpha_0, fig5c offer repeats), the text was corrected and the entry re-run; no outcome changed and none is proposed.

entries.name: mah-2023
entries.title: Distinct value computations in rats' wait times and trial initiation times (Mah et al. 2023)
entries.description: Tests the behavioral findings of Mah, Schiereck, Bossio and Constantinople (2023) on dandiset 001169, which holds 23,034 sessions of 291 rats in a temporal wagering task with hidden reward blocks. It measures the block effects on wait times and trial initiation times, their dynamics at block transitions, their dependence on previous rewards, the effect of the catch probability, sex differences, and simulations of the block inference, inferential and retrospective models. The model comparison fits of Figure 3 were not run (too long), the learning analyses of Figure 4 need sessions that are not in the dandiset, and the pre-cue sessions of Figure 5 are not marked.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Mah et al. (2023) from dandiset 001169
